title: digital presence is a place
content:
from botanical studies of internet magic

listen on apple listen on spotify

hello again, after a few months break. during my retreat, I thought a lot about what being “present” online means. I’ll propose that digital presence isn’t dependent on your labor or content production, but about cultivating a digital container that holds your energy. I’ll explore:

choosing inner rhythms over consistency pressure
freedom from treating yourself as a means of production
embodying the permission to be absent
why content batching doesn’t really work for me
how time works differently on the internet
accumulating wormholes to past selves
digital spaces as vessels for presence

~

I am back on this podcast after more than three months of silence and absence.

I took a three-week trip to visit my family and friends and ended up prolonging that to a two-month stay in the US.

I had to get an unexpected, very minor surgery, and I ended up staying with my family over the holidays.

What was different about this time is that I really gave myself permission to be absent and not create anything, not share anything, not feel the need to remind people that I exist, and I'm so grateful for that period of winter cocooning time because during those two months I really thought a lot about what digital absence means — what does digital presence mean.

In previous episodes I talk a lot about choosing the places we want to share our work on the internet, taking our presence away from platforms and inhabiting our own digital spaces.

the pressure of production

But this episode is not about place, it's about time and rhythm — and do we need to be consistent and where does the pressure to be consistent even come from?

In the months when I was giving myself permission to be silent and absent, I played a fair amount of games on my brother's Nintendo Switch, and there's this one game in which I was a turtle chef making plates of sushi and sashimi for demanding guests.

And as I was playing this game I realized that this is what the hustle of content production and creation down the pipeline can feel like, except instead of getting orders from hungry zombies, we order ourselves, we get orders from our ideas and our internalized pressure.

It's like we are all sushi chefs at one of those sushi bars with the conveyor belts, always feeling time pressure to create new fresh content to be consumed and all of our imaginary audiences are diners.

Maybe we're worried that if we don't keep creating fresh new content they'll forget about us or we'll be irrelevant.

This is exactly the way that platforms and social media is designed to make you feel, to be another means of production, except this time you're working for yourself or you're working for free for the platforms.

creating spaces to hold presence

So instead of being a sushi chef working to fill a conveyor belt of fresh content to be consumed, the model of creation and sharing that I'm continually grounding myself in is that of a builder of a sacred living space.

I actually think about the three of pentacles in the tarot deck in which we have three people looking at what seems to be three pentacles in a church.

One appears to be a priest, the other an architect and the other a builder.

And I've always interpreted this as internal collaboration between different parts of myself working together from my artistic and analytical and spiritual sides to build a mosaic, a tapestry of all of my ideas and art and writings and creative forms.

It's about building layer upon layer an environment that can hold my presence, not producing for the assembly production conveyor belt line, but accumulate over time a living space that is my website, which other people can visit even while technically, I'm absent.

It's the environment itself that holds my presence, not my continual labor.

It's not just that we're told that consistency is the way to build an audience or to have a business.

It's a fear that if we don't show up, we'll be drowned out by the noise.

It's a fear of being forgotten and irrelevant.

personal experiences; recovery from hiding

When I think about my past patterns, when it comes to sharing or not sharing my work, it took me many, many years to find a relative consistent and prolific rhythm of creating and sharing and releasing.

I had to work through years of feeling vulnerable and wanting to hoard my work instead of letting it be in the world.

I would oscillate in the past between sharing my work and feeling overexposed and overwhelmed and then ghosting my audience through not writing that my newsletter for like a year.

My recent consistency and presence was something that I was really proud of.

Therefore, whenever I would go on long trips to visit family, I would feel the pressure to content batch and that is to create lots of content in advance and schedule it in advance so that I could sort of manufacture an illusion of presence even when I was technically absent.

And there's nothing wrong with these kinds of systems.

They work for a lot of businesses.

But I think when your creative work is so tied to your human aliveness, finding the balance between creating from a place of momentum and flow and inspiration versus creating in order to have a concrete output in order to not be forgotten, it's a really fine line to navigate.

I've since understood that content batching doesn't quite work for me because the energy and intention behind what I create seems to carry with it an undertone of pressure.

But of course, this might also change and shift at a later time.

Ultimately, it's about embodying and tuning into natural inner rhythms instead of forcing myself to be consistent for the sake of consistency.

When I realized that my trip had to be almost two months longer than planned, I decided to try an experiment and make this break, this retreat from being in the "public" internet space make it feel deliberate, in that it wasn't about wanting to hide, but about conscious hibernation.

So then the question really becomes, how can I create a space that can be present for others to explore and wander through, even in my own absence?

In other words, how can I be present and absent at the same time?

This is the central theme that I've returned to on this podcast, that when you create a digital space, not as a brochure or showroom of an outdated self, but instead as an environment to inhabit a container to hold an ongoing self, what you're creating is a combination of an archaeological site of personal archives and layered living gardens.

It's building layers upon layers, both fossils and fresh seedlings and growth.

digital time & wormholes to past selves

The past work that you've created, and I have over 600 posts over 10 years, it might feel dead to me, but people stumble upon things I've written years ago and it feels alive and fresh and relevant to them.

I'm grateful that a past aversion of myself can be present for a stranger on the internet.

Time on the internet works differently.

The way that platforms are structured is chronological and dated.

Content becomes stale, sushi becomes stale very fast.

But beyond this chronological feed, a sense of past, present, future can coexist in the same space.

Time can expand and compress, just the way that place also expands and compresses on the internet.

If you approach each thing that you create and share with full presence, then over time you accumulate a universe of wormholes to different selves.

invitations

What would it be like to treat the people who experience your work not as diners in a conveyor belt, but as wanderers in your garden, in your sacred space, in your personal library or your world?

Can each thing that you create and release into the world be a reflection of full presence in your own life?

And how can each piece help create a space that transcends time?

How can you trust in the seasonality and cyclical structures?

How can you be more attuned and trusting of rhythms of your own creative metabolism and give yourself permission to be both fully present and absent?

I think the bigger picture is reminding myself that the way I want to be on the internet is the way I want to be in the world, that is true and authentic and anchored in my own human aliveness.

And that means giving myself permission to take retreats and breaks, and also when I'm feeling a deluge of creative flow and inspiration to let that be true too.

There are so many gifts in the dark, in the silence, in the periods of rest, that reminds me of why this work matters in the first place.

The purpose is being human and being alive.

And this is how your digital presence can feel alive.
